instructions.task: A persuader is chatting with a persuadee to get them to donate to the charity Save the Children. Tag ONLY the final 'Persuader message to tag' with the persuasion strategy or dialogue act it uses. Use the earlier chat only as context (e.g. to tell whether a short reply answers a question or follows a donation commitment).
notes: Pick the single best tag for the message's main function.
Statistics about children's suffering are emotion appeal; facts about the charity itself are credibility appeal.
Short answers to the persuadee's questions, flat fillers, farewells and 'you're welcome' are 'other'-type options.

criteria.greeting: Hello/hi, or the opening how-are-you exchange: asking 'how are you?' or answering it ('I am very good.', 'I'm doing well thank you', 'Doing alright..', 'I'm good, how about you?').
criteria.farewell: Saying goodbye or wishing a good day/night at the end ('Have a great night!', 'I hope you enjoy the rest of your day'), or replying to the other's farewell ('Me too!', 'You too').
criteria.youre-welcome: 'You're welcome' / 'no problem' in reply to thanks.
criteria.filler: Flat, low-content filler, bare yes/ok or bare agreement with no added reaction ('Ok...', 'Fine...', 'yeah..', 'Yes.', 'yes, indeed.', 'Sure.', 'yes, you are correct..', 'Right.').
criteria.answer-to-question: A reply that answers a question the persuadee asked about the persuader themself or the chat ('I have.', 'Yes, I'm familiar with them', 'I am not sure', 'Yes, I think they are great.'), with no new information. Answers giving facts about the charity are credibility appeal; answers about how the donation works are donation information.
criteria.other-misc: Anything else on-task that fits no other option: clarifications, corrections ('sorry, I meant...'), confirming what the persuadee said they will donate, talk about other charities than Save the Children, questions about donation logistics preferences ('Which would you prefer?'), remarks about the HIT/survey mechanics ('we need 10 chats each to complete this hit'), small talk with the persuadee (where they live), the persuader's own job or life when not used to persuade, unclear fragments.
criteria.off-task: Rare: a clear tangent completely unrelated to the charity conversation (e.g. history or politics digressions, unrelated hobbies). NOT small talk questions to the persuadee, NOT the persuader's own job or life, and NOT remarks about the HIT/survey mechanics such as number of chats needed (those are 'other').
criteria.acknowledgement: Engaged agreement, sympathy or reaction to what the persuadee said ('I agree 100%', 'That's great to hear', 'I understand', 'I feel the same', 'Me too', 'That horrifies me!').
criteria.praise-user: Complimenting the persuadee: generous, kind, a good person ('That's awesome and generous!', 'People like you make the world better'); a bare 'Great!' right after the persuadee commits to donate.
criteria.thank: Thanking the persuadee, or expressing gratitude on behalf of the children for their help ('Thank you so much', 'Thanks for your help', 'The children will appreciate it', 'They will be so grateful').
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Directly asking or urging the persuadee to donate or help, including yes/no questions about whether they would donate or take the chance to help, without naming a small amount ('Would you be willing to donate some or all of your payment?', 'Would you take it?', 'Donate some money maybe?', 'You can protect those children if you donate').
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asking how much the persuadee wants to donate ('How much would you like to give?', 'What amount would you feel comfortable donating?').
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Asking for a small or partial amount to get a first commitment, or saying even a little helps ('Every little bit helps', 'May I suggest $.50 or even $1?', 'Any amount is welcome', '$2 you won't miss').
criteria.donation-information: Information about how the donation in this task works: amount range ($0 to $2 / the task payment), deducted from payment, the research team collects and sends it, how to pay, that the persuadee can choose any amount ('It can be as much as you want', 'you can judge it yourself'). (A persuader offering to match or add their own donation is self-modeling, not this.)
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader states their own donation or intention to donate, acting as a role model ('I'm going to donate $2', 'I'll match your $5', 'I usually give to this cause yearly', 'If you donate 30% I will donate 50%', offers to match the persuadee's donation). A passing mention of the persuader's own giving habits in small talk ('i donate every Christmas') is 'other'.
criteria.personal-story: The persuader tells a story about a specific past experience or turning point of their own ('I worked in Africa earlier this year and saw...', 'I decided to be part of the solution since then', 'I have thought about donating before, but never got around to it'). NOT the persuader explaining how or why they gave, or their giving habits in passing (those are 'other'); NOT contrasting their own fortunate life with suffering children (emotion appeal); an anecdote whose point is what the charity does is credibility appeal.
criteria.credibility-appeal: Describing, introducing or praising Save the Children itself: what it is and does, where it works, its history, founder, reputation, ratings, fund-use percentages, results achieved, website links/URLs, answers to 'what do they do?', money it raised, sponsors, awards, that donations are tax deductible.
criteria.emotion-appeal-suffering: Evoking feelings about children's suffering: sad facts and statistics on deaths, war, hunger, disease; 'imagine your own child going through this'; expressing sadness about the children's plight; contrasting one's own fortunate upbringing with these children.
criteria.emotion-appeal-story: A third-person story about a particular child or family who suffered or was helped, or the hope/joy a donation brings to a child.
criteria.logical-appeal: Reasoning that a donation makes a difference ('your donation will help a child', 'they can only help when people donate'), moral reasoning ('children are the future', 'we should all pitch in', 'everyone deserves a chance'), cost comparisons ('less than a cup of coffee').
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asking whether the persuadee knows or has heard of Save the Children or what they know about it ('Have you heard of them?', 'Are you familiar with the organization?').
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asking the persuadee's opinion, feelings, interest or current habits about the charity, the cause or donating ('Is this something you care about?', 'Does this sound like a good charity?', 'What do you think?', 'do you donate to charities?', 'How often do you donate?', 'Have you ever donated to them [Save the Children]?'), or 'Did you know...?' questions about the cause.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asking about the persuadee's past personal experiences or personal life ('Have you ever donated money to a charity before?', 'Have you ever volunteered?', 'Have you sponsored children in the past?', 'Do you have children?'). Asking whether they have donated to Save the Children itself is task-related inquiry.
